Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need a detailed design and implementation plan for a fictional reading club website called the Lantern Room, and i'm trying to get all the pieces into one request because the notes are scattered. the club has about forty members in the fictional town of Bellwether, and it meets twice a month in a room above the public library. members read novels, memoirs, essays, and short story collections, not just one genre. The site is meant to help the group keep track of what it is reading and make the practical details easier to find; it isn't supposed to replace the in-person meetings or turn every discussion into an online forum. Please treat this as a plan for the website, not a finished website, and explain the proposed work in a way a small volunteer committee could review.

The people using it range from members who are comfortable with websites to a few who mostly use email on a phone. A visitor should be able to understand what the club is and when it meets without making an account. Members need a way to see the current selection and upcoming meeting information, and they should be able to add a book to a personal reading list. That last thing is an ordinary permitted action; don't make the whole site sound like members need special permission to use it. The public-facing part should give newcomers a clear first step, but don't invent a membership fee or claim the group is currently accepting applications. We haven't settled either of those details.

For the main screen, I picture the current book and the next meeting near the top, with the club name and a short introduction that sounds welcoming but not salesy. The current selection is “The Summer Book” by Tove Jansson, and the next gathering is listed as Thursday, October 17, at 7:00 p.m. in the library's upstairs room. Keep those details as given. Don't turn the meeting date into a recurring schedule or infer a year. The committee also wants a simple way to find earlier selections, because people often ask what the group read last winter. We have a list of past titles, but this request doesn't include the list, so the plan should say where that history fits without making up entries.

The club coordinator described the tone this way: “The site should feel like a table people can return to, not a noticeboard that shouts at them.” Use that as a clue for the design: calm, readable, and friendly, with no pressure to post or compete for attention. The group has a small lantern mark used on its paper bookmarks, mostly dark green ink on cream paper. It could inform the visual direction, but please don't assume there is a finished logo file or a full set of brand rules. The website should still be legible if the mark isn't available. The plan can discuss the look and layout, but it shouldn't pretend that a designer has already approved mockups.

1. the plan needs to cover these parts, though the notes aren't in a good order yet: the public home page; the current and past reading selections; meeting details; the member reading list; and a basic contact route for someone with a question. Explain what a visitor sees versus what a member sees, without making up a complicated membership system. We have not decided whether member access will use email links, passwords, or some other method, so flag that as an open decision rather than selecting one. Don't specify a database or hosting provider as if we already chose it. A sensible outline of the main screens and the steps a member takes to save a title would be useful.

For the reading list, members should be able to add a title for their own later reading. It is personal, not a public ranking and not a vote on what the club will read next. The selection for club discussion remains something the club announces separately. If the plan mentions what information a saved title could show, stick to ordinary book details such as title and author and distinguish suggestions from settled decisions. There isn't a request here for reviews, comments, star ratings, recommendations between members, or an automated book-matching feature. Please don't quietly turn the simple list into any of those things.

The practical boundary matters because this is a volunteer project with limited time. Describe a first version that concentrates on the stated pages and actions, and separate any genuine open questions from things already in the notes. do not install packages. We are not asking for code to be run or for a live site to be deployed, and no one has picked a technical stack. You can explain implementation considerations in general terms, but don't claim that a particular tool is installed or that a feature has been tested. It would help to mention how the committee could review the plan and confirm decisions, without inventing a launch date or budget.

Please include accessibility and upkeep in a practical way rather than treating them as decorative extras. The site needs clear text, readable contrast, usable headings, and navigation that works for someone on a phone; the brief should connect those points to the club's mixed comfort with technology. The volunteers need to be able to update the next meeting and current title without having to rebuild the whole site. We haven't named the person who will maintain it, and there is no agreed update schedule, so leave those as questions for the committee. Don't promise compliance with a named standard or make claims about testing that hasn't happened.

The final plan should be organized enough to discuss at a committee meeting, with the purpose, audience, pages and actions, visual direction, open decisions, and first-version boundary easy to locate. Include a short numbered section for the main member journey, from finding the current selection to adding a title to a personal reading list, and keep it within the facts above. End with a separate practical note about the unresolved maintenance responsibility and update schedule; that information should not get lost inside the design description. ## Purpose and audience

Members should be able to view the current selection and upcoming meeting information, and add a book to a personal reading list. ## Pages and information

Cover the public home page, current and past reading selections, meeting details, the member reading list, and a basic contact route for questions. Explain what visitors can see and what members can see, without inventing a complicated membership system. The home page should place the club name, a short welcoming but not salesy introduction, the current book, and the next meeting near the top.

Use the current selection and meeting details as given: “The Summer Book” by Tove Jansson; Thursday, October 17, at 7:00 p.m. in the library's upstairs room. Do not infer a year or make the meeting date into a recurring schedule. Include a place for past selections, since members ask what the group read last winter, but do not invent entries for the list that has not been supplied.

Members should be able to add a title to their own reading list for later. The list is personal; it is not a public ranking or a vote on the club’s next selection. The club announces discussion selections separately. If describing information shown for a saved title, use ordinary book details such as title and author, and distinguish suggestions from settled decisions. Do not add reviews, comments, star ratings, member-to-member recommendations, or automated book matching.

## Visual direction

Use a calm, readable, friendly direction that does not pressure people to post or compete for attention. The coordinator described the desired feeling as: “The site should feel like a table people can return to, not a noticeboard that shouts at them.” The club uses a small lantern mark on paper bookmarks, mostly dark green ink on cream paper. It may inform the visual direction, but do not assume a finished logo file or a complete set of brand rules. The site must remain legible without the mark. Discuss look and layout without implying that mockups have already been approved.

## Member journey

Include a short numbered section covering the main member journey, within the information provided:
1. Find the current selection.
2. Add a title to a personal reading list.

Also outline the main screens and the steps a member takes to save a title. Do not decide how member access works: email links, passwords, or another method remain open questions.

## First version and implementation boundaries

Describe a first version focused on the stated pages and actions. Keep implementation considerations general: no technical stack, database, or hosting provider has been chosen. Do not claim that tools are installed, features have been tested, or a site has been deployed. do not install packages. The request is not to run code or deploy a live site. Separate genuine open questions from facts already supplied. Explain how the committee could review the plan and confirm decisions, without inventing a budget or launch date.

Address accessibility and upkeep practically. Include clear text, readable contrast, usable headings, and navigation that works on a phone, connecting these needs to the club’s varied comfort with technology. Volunteers should be able to update the next meeting and current title without rebuilding the whole site. Do not promise compliance with a named standard or claim that unperformed testing has taken place.

Organize the plan so its purpose, audience, pages and actions, visual direction, open decisions, and first-version boundary are easy to locate. End with a separate practical note about the unresolved maintenance responsibility and update schedule.
